target_customer: Software development teams and enterprises that want to host and manage their own Git repositories, then the whole DevOps lifecycle
problem: Teams wanted GitHub style collaboration (merge requests, issues, CI) on their own servers without paying for a closed product, and later wanted one tool instead of a chain of separate DevOps tools.
business_model: Open core: free community edition plus paid self-managed and SaaS tiers per seat, sold to enterprises
product_category: DevOps platform, source code hosting and CI/CD

founders.name: Sid Sijbrandij
founders.background_notes: Joined the open source project around 2012 as a commercial operator and became CEO. Prior employers and education not verified in this research.

founders.name: Dmytro Zaporozhets
founders.background_notes: Created the open source GitLab project in 2011 as a side project to collaborate with his team.

competitors.name: GitHub Enterprise
competitors.what: Self-hosted version of the dominant Git hosting service
competitors.traction_then: GitHub had about 87 percent of respondents in the 2011 Git user survey

competitors.name: Atlassian Stash
competitors.what: Self-hosted Git repository manager from Atlassian

competitors.name: Gitorious
competitors.what: Open source Git hosting site, acquired by GitLab in March 2015 and shut down in June 2015
competitors.traction_then: Second most popular Git host in the 2011 Git user survey at 11.7 percent

technical_complexity.rationale: A Ruby on Rails application wrapping Git with issues, merge requests and later CI runners. Standard engineering with hard parts in scaling Git storage and CI, much of it built by community contributors.

defensibility.rationale: Open source code was copyable, and GitHub had the network. Defensibility came later from enterprise integration across the lifecycle, a large contributor community and the single application bundle.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: GitHub launched its own CI and security features over time and Microsoft bought GitHub in 2018 for $7.5B, but GitLab kept growing and listed on Nasdaq in October 2021.

market_need_then: Strong developer demand for self-hosted Git with GitHub style workflow, shown by an open source project with thousands of contributors and over 10,000 commits before YC, plus enterprise worry about sending code to a third party cloud.

branding.domain_note: Uses gitlab.com as primary domain, which was the company's site by YC time in 2015

identity.logo: Tanuki (Japanese raccoon dog) mark redesigned July 2015 after community feedback, from an angry looking raccoon dog to an abstract one
identity.visual_style: Orange and purple on a clean white site, open and transparent public handbook
identity.voice_and_tone: Direct, transparent and community oriented; public handbook and all remote culture

branding.brand_signature: The tanuki logo and the public company handbook, which GitLab made open in 2015

rebrands.why: Company asked the community for opinions and chose a friendlier mark

branding.community_and_virality: Large open source contributor community; people debate whether the logo is a fox or a tanuki in public issue threads, which shows engagement with the mark.

brand_strength.rationale: The name and tanuki are well known among developers and the company built a strong transparency brand, though the name resembles GitHub and the tanuki is often mistaken for a fox.

pivots.from: Self-hosted Git hosting alternative to GitHub
pivots.to: Single application covering the whole DevOps lifecycle
pivots.why: Expansion strategy to compress cycle time across plan, build, test and deploy, announced with the 2017 Series C

outcome_analysis: GitLab succeeded by turning a popular open source GitHub alternative into an enterprise DevOps platform. It raised steadily from a $1.5M seed in 2015 through $268M in 2019, was valued in the billions, and listed on Nasdaq in October 2021. Success came from a large contributor community, open core pricing, an all remote cost advantage and the move to a single application for the whole lifecycle, while GitHub remained a larger rival.
notes: Seed 2015-07 amount and investor and the Series D 2018 amount and $1.1B valuation come from aggregators only and are unverified. Series A investor sources disagree (Khosla Ventures vs Right Side Capital). Series B is listed as $18.8M by one aggregator. Series E 2019 valuation ranges $2.7B to $2.8B. IPO proceeds vary $637M to $801M depending on primary or secondary shares. Founder prior employers and education were not verified. Series A date from YC page headline; company says Series B in 2016 announced September.
